findings.summary: The comparison table lists rules in an order that conflicts with the precedence list that follows it, and the precedence words are bare, unlabeled fragments.
findings.evidence:
Table rows run "new? | new", "call/apply/bind? | explicit", "obj.? | implicit", "plain? | default"; then "new
highest
explicit
implicit
default
lowest"
findings.fix: Label the precedence block as 'Precedence (high to low)' and render it as a single ordered line or a small ladder diagram: new > explicit > implicit > default.

findings.summary: Code example is shown without a stated one-line idea before it, and the 'Read the call' flow is plain text where a flowchart would help.
findings.evidence: "const a = { b: { n: 'b', fn() { return this.n } } }\na.b.fn()  // 'b': this is b, not a" and "Look at the call, not the definition: new? call/apply/bind? obj.? plain?"
findings.fix: Put the rule 'only the object immediately left of the dot counts' directly before the code, and present the four questions as a decision flow diagram.

findings.summary: The 'new' steps are fragments in a diagram-like list without a clear order, and one bullet holds several ideas.

linked to Fn.prototype
Run Fn
this = that object
Return it

findings.summary: The 'lost this' example shows code before the idea, and the explanation comes only after the code.
findings.evidence: "setTimeout(obj.method, 0);            // this lost" followed later by "Why it breaks"
findings.fix: State 'a bare method reference loses obj at call time' first, then show the code.

findings.summary: The chain diagram is an unlabeled list of nodes, and the code example mixes three checks into one console.log line with no stated idea first.
findings.fix: Draw the chain with arrows (obj -> Fn.prototype -> Object.prototype -> null) and split the console.log lines, each with a comment naming what it shows.

findings.summary: A single bullet holds multiple ideas.
findings.evidence: "Object.create(proto) sets the prototype; Object.create(null) gives a chainless dictionary"
findings.fix: Split into two bullets, one for Object.create(proto) and one for Object.create(null).

findings.summary: Bullets pack several ideas, and the hoisting row of the table is misleading shorthand.
findings.evidence: "class A { m() {} } puts m on A.prototype: shared, non-enumerable"; "Field handle = () => {...} is an own property, per instance"; "Hoisting | usable early | TDZ"
findings.fix: Split the bullets into one idea each, and write the row as 'function: hoisted and usable early; class: in the temporal dead zone (ReferenceError before the declaration)'.

findings.summary: The first bullet holds several ideas and mixes in an unrelated fix, and the code is shown with its explanation placed after it.
findings.evidence: "Falls to default: undefined in strict mode, so this.x throws TypeError"; "arr.forEach(function(){ this }) also gets default binding"; "thisArg is the second argument of forEach"
findings.fix: Give each point its own bullet, state the thisArg fix before the code, and fold the closing line into the fix bullet.

findings.summary: Page 'New and prototypes' mixes two distinct mistakes with no visual, and 'No new' is stated vaguely.
findings.evidence: "No new: sloppy mode sets properties on the global object"; "Fn.prototype.list = [] is shared by all instances"
findings.fix: Put both mistakes in the Mistake | Why | Fix table, with the no-new case stating that this falls to the global object, and show a small shared-vs-per-instance picture.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet uses inconsistent terms for the same thing, calling the lookup link both [[Prototype]] and 'prototype', and 'ctx' versus 'enclosing this'.
findings.evidence: "extends links both prototype and static chain"; "Object.getPrototypeOf(o) reads the link; Object.create(p) sets it"
findings.fix: Use '[[Prototype]]' for the link and 'Fn.prototype' for the property throughout, e.g. 'extends links B.prototype to A.prototype and B to A'.
